title: Humility after learning
hook: and above every possessor of knowledge is one more knowing (12:76)

segments.voice: Yesterday, gratitude for the ordinary, and your line: untitled teachers. Did your sentence of thanks reach the person you thought of? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-five.

"And over every lord of knowledge there is one more knowing." That is half a verse from the Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation, and it turns up in the middle of a family drama. Yusuf, now powerful in Egypt, has had a royal cup hidden in his brother's bag, so that he can keep him close. The plan works. And right there, the verse says the plan was Allah's doing for Yusuf, then steps back and adds: there is always someone who knows more. After a year of learning, today is about that sentence.
screen: `OVER EVERY LORD OF KNOWLEDGE…` → `YUSUF, THE CUP, THE BROTHER'S BAG.` → `ONE MORE KNOWING.`

segments.voice: First, the verse itself. Its full line says that Allah raises by degrees whom He will, and then: over every lord of knowledge there is one more knowing. Knowledge is real, and it lifts people. It also never reaches a top shelf that a human can stand on. Second, a prophet learns it. Five days ago, Musa set out for the meeting of the two seas. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari tells how that journey began. Musa is asked who is the most learned of people, and he answers: I am. Allah reproaches him, in the hadith's telling, because he did not refer the knowledge back to Allah, and tells him of a servant who knows more than he does. In the Qur'an Musa asks that servant, in paraphrase: may I follow you, so that you teach me some of the right guidance you were taught? A prophet becomes a student again. Third, even the angels say it. When Adam is taught the names, the angels answer, in paraphrase: glory be to You, we have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Fourth, the words people use. Muslim teachers may close an answer with Allahu a'lam, Allah knows best. And a story people tell about Imam Malik has him answering question after question in one sitting with: I don't know. Whether or not every detail of that story holds, the habit it praises is the one in the verse. Four years of lessons, in the verse's own terms, are a step, not the summit. Someone knows more, and above them, someone more again.
screen: `RAISED BY DEGREES, NEVER AT THE TOP.` · `MUSA SAYS I, THEN WALKS TO LEARN.` · `THE ANGELS: ONLY WHAT YOU TAUGHT US.` · `ALLAH KNOWS BEST. I DON'T KNOW.`

segments.voice: The practice: admit what you don't know. Settle into the sit, and breathe. Look for one thing from this year that you've been talking about as if you were sure, a ruling, a story, a meaning, and you're not. Name it to yourself plainly: I don't actually know this. Notice what it's like to say that. Then let it rest. If you pray, you can add the words Muslims use, Allahu a'lam, Allah knows best. If not, just let the not-knowing be true for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Humility after learning. The more you learn, the clearer it gets that over every lord of knowledge is one more knowing. Today's word.
Your line: someone knows more. Today, say I don't know out loud, once, when it's true, and then ask who might. Tomorrow, year four close: the ways. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Muslim scholars and teachers end a ruling or an answer with Allahu a'lam, Allah knows best, and students are taught to say I don't know rather than guess about the religion.

fork.setup: you are Musa. someone asks: who is the most learned of people? what do you answer?
fork.reveal: in Sahih al-Bukhari Musa says I am, and Allah reproaches him for not referring the knowledge back to Allah, then sends him to learn from someone who knows more.

original.note: Arabic: one who knows; the last word of the line in 12:76, and al-'Alim, the All-Knowing, is a name of Allah.

trapdoor: what you thought: learning is about getting to the top.
what it means: every knower has someone above them, and the learned are the ones who keep saying so.
what a scholar hears: wa fawqa kulli dhi 'ilmin 'alim (12:76), Musa's 'I' in Bukhari's hadith of al-Khidr, and the angels' 'no knowledge except what You taught us' (2:32).
